newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs end sharply down after BOJ rate report.
newsitem.headline: JGBs end sharply down after BOJ rate report.

text.p: Key December Japanese government bond futures lost half a point on Friday, due to a media report which said the Bank of Japan is concerned about any excessive decline in long-term interest rates.
A BOJ spokesman told Reuters that the central bank would not comment on the media report.
"The BOJ is worried that long-term interest rates are falling excessively," Jiji news agency reported.
Jiji did not provide a source for its report.
The December fell sharply to end at 121.45, compared to 121.95 on Thursday.
"When the report about the BOJ's comment on long-term interest rates came out, the December was sold suddenly, falling to as low as 121.34," said a brokerage trader.
The December had fluttered near 121.80 for much of the day before dropping sharply on the media report.
The key futures contract moved within a range of 121.34 to 122.07 during the day.
Earlier, traders said market sentiment had been dampened by selling of cash JGBs which took place the previous day.

"The market is carrying over the weak sentiment from Thursday. When the December tried and failed to stay above 122.00 in the morning, it became a seller's market," said a trader for another brokerage.
Selling of cash JGBs was detected on Friday as well, as types such as those in the 160 range were sold, traders said.

"Traders seem to be staying away from cash JGBs in the 160 and 170 range, since they seem expensive compared to other cash JGBs," said a trader for a city bank's securities affiliate. Demand for municipal and government-guaranteed bonds was weak, traders said.

"The 2.9 percent coupon rate is deemed too low for government-guaranteed and municipal bonds, and market participants have shown a preference for JGBs instead, because of it," said a city bank trader.
The benchmark 182nd cash JGB was yielding 2.875 percent as of 0716 GMT, up from Thursday's 2.850 percent.
The dissolution of the Lower House of parliament has had little impact on the market so far, traders said.
